messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 67

# The Weight of the Scan

Mei Lin is a 42-year-old Malaysian-born woman who works as a senior project manager at a mid-sized construction firm. She is married to her husband of fourteen years, and by most outward measures, her life looks ordered and purposeful. She is the kind of person who color-codes her calendars and builds contingency plans into every project timeline. She has always believed that if you prepare carefully enough, things will not fall apart.

Two years ago, a routine check-up revealed a mass in her left lung. Within a week, she was sitting in an oncologist's office hearing the word *malignant*. The weeks that followed moved in a blur of biopsies, staging appointments, and hushed phone calls to her parents back in Kuala Lumpur. She underwent surgery and an aggressive course of chemotherapy. For eight months, her body — the body she had always trusted to simply function — became the site of something she could not manage or plan around. There were nights in the hospital when she genuinely did not know if she would wake up. Her husband slept in the chair beside her bed so many times that the nurses learned his coffee order.

The cancer is now in remission. Her oncologist uses the word *cured* with cautious optimism. Her colleagues threw her a small welcome-back lunch when she returned to work. On paper, the crisis is over.

Mei Lin does not experience it that way.

She wakes most mornings between three and four o'clock with her heart already pounding, certain — in those first disoriented seconds — that she is back in the hospital. The smell of antiseptic on her husband's hands from his own work as a pharmacist can send her into a sudden, cold stillness that she cannot explain to him without feeling ashamed. She finds herself scanning her body constantly throughout the day: a twinge in her side, a cough that lingers two days too long, a bruise she cannot account for. Each one opens a trapdoor beneath her.

At work, she functions — she is meticulous about that — but the effort costs her enormously. She manages large, complex projects with multiple moving parts, and she has always drawn a quiet confidence from that competence. Now she sits in risk-assessment meetings and feels a strange, dissociated dread, as though the language of contingency and failure has become personal in a way she cannot separate from herself. She builds redundancies into every plan, not because the project demands it, but because some part of her is convinced that the moment she stops anticipating disaster, it will arrive.

She has stopped joining colleagues for lunch. She declined her sister's invitation to visit in Singapore twice, telling her the timing was difficult. The truth is that the idea of being far from her hospital, her oncologist, her known geography, fills her with a panic she cannot rationalize away. She carries her most recent scan results in her handbag. She is not sure when she started doing that.

Her husband tries. He is gentle and patient, and she knows he is frightened too, in his own way. But when he touches her scar — even tenderly — she pulls away. The scar is not a reminder of survival to her. It is a reminder of how quickly the ground disappeared.

What troubles Mei Lin most, when she is honest with herself, is the sense that the person who color-coded her calendars and believed in preparation no longer fully exists. She did everything right. She went to her appointments, she ate well, she did not smoke. And still, her body made plans of its own. She sits with that knowledge every single day, and she does not yet know what to do with a world that turned out to be that indifferent to her readiness.
